name: Belief perseverance
statement: A belief built on evidence that is later shown to be wholly fabricated does not return to where it started.
meaning: The claim is narrower than "people resist argument". It concerns the one case where the normative answer is not in doubt: every scrap of evidence behind a belief is revealed to the believer as invented, and the belief should therefore revert to its prior state. Anderson, Lepper and Ross set out that reasoning in 1980, noting that everyday disputes rarely permit anyone to say how much revision an attack warrants, while total discrediting does. What the experiments measure is the residue after that discrediting. Two things are being measured across the literature. One is self-perception, where false feedback on a rigged task shapes what people think of their own ability. The other is a general theory about how two variables relate, held by someone with no stake in the answer. Siebert and Siebert define the modern version as opinions that persevere after the information behind them has been retracted, and separate it from the continued influence effect, which concerns retracted facts still feeding inferential reasoning about an event.

origin.who: Lee Ross, Mark R. Lepper and Michael Hubbard
origin.where: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
origin.note: Their paper reported two experiments in a debriefing paradigm and concluded that process debriefing, unlike standard outcome debriefing, generally eliminated the erroneous self-perceptions. The phrase in the title is "perseverance in self-perception and social perception"; Anderson, Lepper and Ross called it theory perseverance in 1980, and Anderson used the words belief perseverance in 1983.

evidence: Ross, Lepper and Hubbard ran Experiment 1 on 60 female high school juniors and seniors recruited by newspaper advertisement for $2. Each examined 25 cards, each carrying one real and one fictitious suicide note, and was told she had scored 24 (success), 17 (average) or 10 (failure). After a delay of 5 or 25 minutes the experimenter explained that the score had been fixed in advance. Estimates of past and future performance still tracked the discredited feedback, F(1, 54) = 16.07 for own past performance minus estimated average performance. Experiment 2 used 144 female Stanford undergraduates, 72 acting and 72 watching as yoked observers, with data from a further 24 unobserved actors set aside. Actors given no debriefing estimated 22.75 correct after success feedback and 9.50 after failure. Outcome debriefing moved those to 18.33 and 12.83. Process debriefing, which added a discussion of the perseverance mechanism itself, moved them to 16.50 and 15.17. Anderson, Lepper and Ross switched the object from self-image to a social theory. Seventy Stanford undergraduates read two case studies suggesting that risk taking either predicted or undermined success as a firefighter. Before debriefing the manipulation produced F(1, 63) = 20.21 on a composite belief measure. After subjects were told the cases were fictitious it produced F(1, 63) = 17.43, and the reduction was not statistically reliable, F(1, 63) = 1.59. Their second experiment ran 62 subjects and analysed 60, in cells of ten. Within its no-explanation conditions debriefing did dampen the beliefs, interaction F(1, 54) = 23.31. It still left them apart in both the debriefing-explanation, F(1, 54) = 69.74, and debriefing-no-explanation, F(1, 54) = 19.24, conditions.

replication.headline: Siebert and Siebert re-ran the firefighter paradigm on 366 people and found opinions still displaced from baseline after retraction, d = 0.80.
replication.detail: The residue survives repetition, in the original paradigm and in newer ones. Anderson repeated the firefighter paradigm himself in 1982 on 88 undergraduates, and the beliefs of subjects shown one side only survived debriefing, F(1, 80) = 32.30. His 1983 study gave 98 undergraduates either two case histories or a statistical summary of 20 firefighters, matched for the strength of the belief they induced, and debriefed everyone. Perseverance was present at once, F(1, 90) = 28.43, and a week later, F(1, 84) = 23.53, though at a week only the case-history group still showed it. Siebert and Siebert used the same firefighter topic with a fabricated study summary and two case studies, measuring opinions before misinformation, after it, after retraction and after a debiasing treatment. Of 366 participants, 312 (85%) shifted after the misinformation and 251 (68.5% of the total sample) were still displaced from their own baseline after the retraction, d = 0.80. Their 2024 study moved to a real-world topic, a fabricated blog article about remote versus in-office work. There 504 of 876 participants (58%) shifted, and 364 (42%) remained displaced after retraction, d = 0.52. Greenspan and Loftus tested the same logic on memory rather than opinion. In their Study 1, 373 participants watched a video, some received misinformation and were then debriefed; a week later the misinformation effect was still there, at phi = .12 on one critical item and phi = .15 on the other. Miketta and Friese ran six studies in which participants received false feedback about their intelligence or their attractiveness and likability. Their abstract reports that lower well-being and more hostile attributions survived written debriefing, in-person debriefing and a self-affirming essay, with affective consequences lasting two weeks and longer. It also reports that every debriefing version reduced those effects to some degree, and that the longest in-person debriefing worked best. No multi-laboratory replication project has taken the effect on. Crossref and PubMed were searched for one on 21 September 2026 and returned none.

study.cite: Siebert, J., & Siebert, J. U. (2023). Effective mitigation of the belief perseverance bias after the retraction of misinformation: Awareness training and counter-speech. PLOS ONE, 18(3), e0282202.

limits: The mechanism has held up worse than the effect. Anderson, Lepper and Ross attributed perseverance to the causal explanations people build, reporting a point-biserial correlation of .44 between the presence of a general explanatory principle in a subject's writing and the degree of postdebriefing perseverance. Anderson then failed to reproduce that effect twice in his own laboratory. His 1982 study found perseverance no stronger in the explanation than in the no-explanation conditions, F(1, 80) < 1. His 1983 study asked about half its subjects to write explanations and found no effect of doing so in either session, F values below 1, which he called contrary to previous findings. The effect is also not irreversible, and every study that has tried a better debriefing has moved it. Ross, Lepper and Hubbard's process debriefing nearly closed the gap in 1975. Anderson's counterexplanation and inoculation procedures cut perseverance in 1982, F(1, 80) = 5.06, but left a residue, F(1, 80) = 6.26. Greenspan and Loftus wrote an enhanced debriefing that named the misinformation and explained how memory errors arise, and in their Study 2 it removed the effect on one critical item. Siebert and Siebert found counter-speech brought opinions back to within 0.12 of baseline on a seven-point scale, a difference that was not statistically reliable. They add that their equivalence test did not confirm the two were the same, so elimination is suggested there rather than shown. Anglin, Rath, Yuodsnukis and Miller ran three preregistered experiments on capital punishment, gun control, and video games and aggression. Their abstract reports that participants shifted their beliefs towards the evidence and held the shift the next day, mainly among those shown belief-inconsistent evidence. That is the opposite paradigm and close to the opposite result, and the article itself could not be read for this entry. On 21 September 2026 the publisher answered every request with a Cloudflare challenge, HTTP 403, on the landing page and on the CC BY PDF alike. DOAJ, Europe PMC, CORE, Unpaywall, OpenAlex, eScholarship and the Wayback Machine hold no other copy, and the authors' OSF project holds materials and data only. The figures behind that abstract are left off this page. McFarland, Cheam and Buehler published a replication and extension of the debriefing paradigm in 2007. It is subscription-only, and on 21 September 2026 the publisher's page answered a bot filter with HTTP 403, so nothing from it is reported here. No meta-analysis of belief perseverance was located. Crossref and PubMed were searched on 21 September 2026 and returned meta-analyses of debunking, of the continued influence effect and of psychological debriefing, not of this literature. The two 1975 experiments used only female participants, and both 1980 experiments used Stanford undergraduates in cells of about ten. The social-theory branch has been repeated most, and much of that work is Anderson's own. The one direct replication of the 1975 self-perception paradigm is the paper that could not be read.
misreadings: Belief perseverance is not the continued influence effect, and Siebert and Siebert draw the line by paradigm. Belief perseverance gives people information on a topic, retracts it, then asks their opinion on the topic. The continued influence paradigm gives people pieces of a developing event, retracts one, then asks open-ended inference questions and watches them reach for the retracted piece. Greenspan and Loftus note that the two names are applied to closely related procedures, so the boundary is a matter of what is measured rather than a difference in kind. Neither is the backfire effect, which requires the correction to push belief further in the wrong direction; perseverance means the correction does less than it should, not less than nothing. The line most often overstated is that debriefing does not work. Ross, Lepper and Hubbard's own abstract says process debriefing generally eliminated the erroneous self-perceptions, and their conclusion was addressed to the ethics of deception research rather than to human stubbornness in general. Greenspan and Loftus are a caution in the other direction: their enhanced debriefing wiped out the effect on the question about what was stolen, chi-square 0.28 in that group of 148, and left it intact on the question about the jacket, phi = .17.
